space.reading: The question behind every number here is how many independent directions the orders really span. Ten columns are numeric as the script parses them — including customer_id, zip and late, which the typing above takes out of the arithmetic — and they are of full rank: no column is an exact linear combination of the others, so the redundancy the file carries is not linear. The variance says more: 95 % of it lives in six directions, and the two-nearest-neighbour estimate, which measures the dimension of the surface the points actually lie on, is about seven. That gap between ten columns and seven dimensions is the signature of products and lookups — total is unit_price times qty, not a sum — and it is what the derivations below go and name.

basis.reading: Having found that the space is smaller than the table, the next question is which columns span it. The basis — the columns no rule derives from the others — has eight members against an intrinsic dimension near seven. The surplus of about one is weight_kg: it is not derivable, yet it moves almost in step with qty, because every item weighs roughly the same. A basis that size is honest; a smaller one would have to pretend that weight is a function of quantity, which the data refutes on its residuals.

disagreements.evidence: pearson 0.966 and nmi 0.6272 with qty; not derivable (no fit reaches R² 0.999)
disagreements.reading: The script sees weight move with quantity and the meaning says why without making it a rule: an order weighs its item count times a per-item weight the file does not carry. That hidden unit weight is a dimension of its own, so weight_kg stays in the basis — and a model will see two nearly parallel inputs.

disagreements.evidence: linear_derivability marks subtotal formula_ambiguous: its degree-2 regressors are mutually dependent
disagreements.reading: The script establishes that subtotal is derivable but spreads the coefficients across total and unit_price*qty, which are the same column; the canonical formula is the semantic channel's, and the rule states it.

pairs.independence: definitional, not statistical: no rule links them, yet the data puts them on nearly one line
definitional and statistical: price and quantity are chosen by different people and barely move together
definitional and, on this file, statistical: no season makes deliveries slower

orthogonality.reading: With the basis settled, the remaining question is whether its members are independent only by definition or in the data as well. Almost every pair is both: normalized mutual information stays below 0.05. The one exception is qty and weight_kg, independent by definition and nearly collinear in the data — the hidden unit weight again — and it is the pair a linear model would stumble on.
